name: Freedom
tagline: Cross-device website and app blocking for focused work

pricing.notes: Official pricing page reviewed; taxes, promotions, and regional pricing may differ.

tiers.name: Free
tiers.limits: Unlimited devices, cross-device sync, and custom blocklists; the public page does not state a numeric session-count or duration cap.

tiers.name: Premium
tiers.limits: Unlimited blocking sessions, including sessions longer than 2 hours, across all supported devices.

tiers.name: Forever
tiers.limits: Lifetime Premium access across supported devices.
tiers.notes: Current one-time promotional price $99.50; regular price shown as $199.

pricing.freeTierCaps: Unlimited devices, cross-device sync, and custom blocklists; numeric session limits are not published.
pricing.hiddenCosts: The $3.33 figure on file is the annual-billing equivalent, not the month-to-month price of $8.99. The $99.50 lifetime price is a current 50%-off promotion rather than the displayed $199 regular price.

verdictSummary: The visible distraction blocking loop is buildable, but a credible replacement needs more than the first screen. Freedom earns its keep through polish, OS integration, so expect a weekend or multi-day build and a narrower personal scope.
coreLoopDIY: Build a local desktop utility that captures the essential distraction blocking workflow with keyboard-first controls and local storage.
replacementScope: narrow personal or very small-team substitute
requirements: macOS, Windows, or Linux development machine
Local filesystem access and OS permissions
whyPeopleStillPay: Freedom: People keep paying because a utility used dozens of times a day must be instant, predictable, and compatible with every OS update.
ongoingBurden: Track OS permission changes, shortcut conflicts, packaging, code signing, and regressions after system updates.

priorArt.name: ActivityWatch
priorArt.desc: Local-first automatic time tracking with an extensible event model.

alternatives.name: Apple Screen Time
alternatives.desc: Already installed on Apple devices, syncs limits, and is easier to override than Freedom.

alternatives.name: ScreenZen
alternatives.desc: App and site blocking across phones and desktops, paid for by donations instead of guilt.

rejectedAlternatives.name: Cold Turkey Blocker
rejectedAlternatives.desc: The free tier blocks websites; app blocking and schedules are the paid product.

rejectedAlternatives.name: LeechBlock NG
rejectedAlternatives.desc: Excellent browser blocker; it cannot block desktop or phone apps, so it misses the cross-device core.

notes: Useful boundary case: the first 60 percent of Freedom is approachable, but operating the last 40 percent is the real subscription.
prompt:
Build a deliberately narrow personal substitute for Freedom, not a full clone.
Use exactly this stack: Tauri 2 + React + TypeScript + SQLite.
Primary job: Build a local desktop utility that captures the essential distraction blocking workflow with keyboard-first controls and local storage.
Start from an empty folder and create the complete working project.
Make the default mode single-user and private.
Store user data locally unless the core job requires the declared self-hosted database.
Do not add analytics, telemetry, ads, or third-party accounts.
Put every secret and external credential in .env and provide .env.example.
Use realistic sample data that is clearly labelled and easy to delete.
Implement the smallest polished interface that completes the core loop end to end.
Include clear empty, loading, validation, success, and failure states.
Add import and export so the user is not trapped in the app.
Use accessible keyboard navigation, labels, focus states, and sensible contrast.
Validate untrusted input and never log secrets or private file contents.
Deliberately exclude these paid-product advantages: polished shortcuts and accessibility; vendor-maintained updates; cross-device sync.
Do not fake integrations, network effects, proprietary data, model quality, compliance, or security claims.
Where an external API is optional, keep the app useful without it and explain the degraded mode.
Write focused unit tests for the data model and the most important workflow.
Add one end-to-end smoke test that proves the core loop works.
Create a README with setup, permissions, architecture, data location, backup, and limitations.
Add scripts for install, development, test, build, and a production-style local run.
Run the tests and build before finishing, then fix errors rather than merely describing them.
